text: A saucer of milk set down in a room is usually put out for a small animal.
exceptions: It may be left over from someone's own use, or put down for a stray.

text: Boots on a chair seat leave scuffs or dirt of a kind that sitting on it does not.
exceptions: Objects set on a seat, or ordinary wear, can also mark it.

text: A lash is left straight or loosely coiled so that it can be used as a whip; tied fast into a loop, it no longer can be.
exceptions: A loop may be a way of hanging it up, or a makeshift repair.

text: India is known for venomous snakes whose bite can bring pain, collapse and death within hours while leaving only tiny punctures.
exceptions: Most snakes are harmless, and many bites do not kill.

text: Popular tales, especially from India, have snakes drinking milk put out for them.
exceptions: This is folklore, and milk is not a snake's natural food.

reads: a large iron safe
text: Roylott's room is plainly furnished, and its most striking contents are a large iron safe.

reads: a small wooden shelf full of books, mostly of a technical character
text: He keeps a shelf of mostly technical books, presumably medical, though Watson does not say.
The clang has been unexplained since the shutter bar failed. A large iron safe in the next room is the first thing we have met that could make a noise like a mass of metal.

reads: were the principal things which met the eye
text: No bottles, chemical apparatus, cage or hutch are listed. That is awkward for a vapour made here and for any openly kept creature, though 'principal things' leaves room for smaller items.

reads: What’s in here?
text: After going round everything, the one object he asks about is the safe.

reads: Only once, some years ago.
text: 'Business papers' rests on one look years ago. She was just as flat about the bell-rope going to the housekeeper's room, and that was an assumption. What is in the safe now is unknown.

reads: There isn’t a cat in it, for example?
text: An absurd thing to ask about a safe, as Helen says. Yet he has raised the idea of something alive being kept in the iron box, and he rarely asks idle questions.

reads: a small saucer of milk which stood on the top of it
text: A small saucer of milk is standing on top of the safe.

reads: we don’t keep a cat
text: The household has no cat.
Milk in a house with no cat, and in Roylott's own room. Something small is probably being fed here, and Helen does not seem to know of it.

reads: a saucer of milk does not go very far in satisfying its wants
text: The milk is not for the cheetah. Holmes does not mention the baboon, but it too roams the grounds and is far too big for a ventilator. Any creature that matters is one we have not been told about.

The creature option moves ahead. Roylott is sent Indian animals, and something small may be kept in this room, perhaps in the safe, that could pass the ventilator and use the rope to reach the pillow.
options: A small creature kept here reaches the bed by ventilator and rope
The milk is for some harmless pet and means nothing
The milk is bait or carries poison
hindsight: Nobody has joined the milk to the ventilator. A first-time reader must put together Holmes's joke about a cat, the Indian animals and the rope as a route.

reads: examined the seat of it with the greatest attention
text: What can the seat of a plain wooden chair tell him?
options: Someone has been standing on it
An animal has been on it
Something has been stood or spilled there

text: The rope's hook is just above the opening, and a bell-rope normally starts high on the wall, so the ventilator is probably out of easy reach. Roylott has an armchair to sit in. Boot marks on the hard chair would mean he stands on it to get at something high, such as his end of the opening.
hindsight: Holmes does not say what he saw, and Watson gives neither the opening's height nor which wall the chair is against. The reader has to supply all of this.

text: A living thing cannot be relied on. Julia heard the whistle for several nights before the night she died, and Helen came through last night unharmed. A method that fails on some nights would fit a creature better than a dose or a device.
On the fatal night the order was scream, whistle, then a clang moments later. If something lives in the safe, the whistle may call it back and the clang may be the safe door shutting on it.
options: The whistle recalls the creature and the safe door clangs
The whistle is a signal to some person and the clang has another source
hindsight: Nothing yet shows that anything is kept in the safe or responds to a whistle. The reader must combine Holmes's joke with the order of sounds Helen reported two years after the event.

text: What small Indian creature could use a rope, be taken for a 'speckled band', and kill with convulsions and no visible marks? A patterned venomous snake would meet every one of those conditions.
options: A small mammal used in some other way
hindsight: This is far easier if the ending is known. A first-time reader must take 'band' as a description of something living and notice that a body with 'no marks' could still have tiny punctures.

reads: That is quite settled
text: He went to the chair with one point to determine, and he has his answer. We are not told what it was.

reads: The lash, however, was curled upon itself and tied so as to make a loop of whipcord.
text: A small dog lash hanging on the bed has been tied into a loop.
No dog has been mentioned at Stoke Moran. Helen's list of the beasts is a cheetah and a baboon, so why is a dog lash by his bed?
Tied like this it can no longer be used as a whip. It has been made into something else: a ready noose or loop.
A loop of cord is literally a band. Could this be what Julia meant, or a noose used on her?
options: The loop is the band she saw
It is a noose that was used on her

text: Neither will do. Plain whipcord is not speckled, nobody could get into the room to use it, and a noose would have left marks on a body that had none.
If it was never used on a person, a loop on a short handle may be for controlling or lifting something the owner does not want to touch.
options: A noose for handling a dangerous creature
A restraint for something else in the house

text: The snake guess takes in the new details. Popular tales give snakes milk, and a noose on a short handle would suit an animal one dares not grasp.
hindsight: This needs the folk belief about snakes and milk, and the prior guess of a snake. Holmes has said nothing to point this way.

reads: when a clever man turns his brains to crime it is the worst of all
text: The looped lash draws from him a remark about crime and a clever man. He has stopped testing and speaks as if he knows what was done here, and he credits Roylott with brains and not just rage.
I give up the idea that Roylott is only a loud distraction. The false fittings were put in his house, Helen calls him cunning, and Holmes now speaks of a clever criminal.

reads: I think that I have seen enough now
text: He has seen enough, yet Watson has not reported the far end of the ventilator. That it opens into this room is still only our inference, however good.

reads: I had never seen my friend’s face so grim or his brow so dark
text: He laughed at the poker, but this room has made him grim. What he found is worse than the threats.

reads: Your life may depend upon your compliance.
text: Holmes now says outright that her life is at stake, and he treats the danger as immediate.

reads: both my friend and I must spend the night in your room
text: Holmes and Watson are to spend the night in the middle room.
The tooth-brush and the dismissed trap meant what they seemed to mean: he always expected to stay the night.

This goes beyond 'lock yourself up' and Harrow only if he turns violent. Having seen the rooms, Holmes means to be in the room himself when it happens, which answers why she was not simply taken away.

reads: Certainly.
text: The Crown is in sight of the house and its windows can be seen from there, so 'opposite' was fair enough. It also gives Holmes a place to watch from.

reads: put your lamp there as a signal to us
text: Once Roylott has retired, Helen is to set her lamp in the window as a signal.

reads: withdraw quietly with everything which you are likely to want into the room which you used to occupy
text: Helen is to leave the middle room quietly and spend the night in her old room.

reads: you must open the shutters of your window, undo the hasp
text: They will wait at the inn for the lamp and come in by the window. Since he has shown that barred shutters cannot be passed from outside, she has to open them.

She is safer in a room with a pierced wall than behind a locked door in the middle room. Holmes's plan accepts that locks do not answer this danger, and it treats the danger as belonging to that room.

reads: on pretence of a headache
text: The headache keeps her away from a man who knows she went to Holmes and has already bruised her. It also lets him go on thinking she is where he expects her to be, in the middle room.
To reach that window at night they must cross grounds where a cheetah and a baboon wander freely. Holmes has not mentioned them.

reads: we shall investigate the cause of this noise which has disturbed you
text: 'This noise' is a mild way to put it just after 'your life may depend'. He is keeping his real idea from her.

reads: Perhaps I have.
text: He all but admits he has the answer, and we have been shown what he looked at: rope, ventilator, safe, milk, chair and lash.

reads: I should prefer to have clearer proofs before I speak.
text: Even with his client begging, he will not name it. He regards what he has as short of proof, so tonight is the test of it.

reads: I think that there was probably some more tangible cause
text: Helen's death by pure fright can go. Holmes rejects it, and it never explained what could have frightened her in a sealed room.
'Tangible' tells against fumes as well as fright. It suits a physical agent that reached her through the opening, though he says only 'probably'.

reads: if Dr. Roylott returned and saw us our journey would be in vain
text: Being seen would ruin the plan, so the plan needs Roylott to go about his night as usual. Holmes wants whatever happens in that room to happen, with himself there in place of Helen.
Roylott knows Holmes has been consulted, and a cunning man might lie low. Holmes is staking the night on his going ahead anyway, perhaps because the wedding is close and Helen may talk.

Tonight, at about three, in the middle room: a low whistle, and something coming through the ventilator and down the rope to the pillow. If the safe guess is right, a metallic clang from next door should go with it.

Open: what came through the opening; what the 'speckled band' is; what is really in the safe; who or what the milk is for; what Holmes saw on the chair; what the looped lash is for; what the whistle and the clang are; how Roylott found Baker Street; what his business in town was; and whether the money would survive Helen's death.

Working picture: Roylott made the false ventilator and rope as a route from his room to the pillow, and he has moved Helen onto it. Something tangible travels that way at night, most likely a small creature kept and fed in his room, with the whistle and safe perhaps part of the routine. Holmes will take Helen's place tonight. Helen probably survives, and Roylott's advertised death may now be close.
options: A small venomous creature sent through the ventilator
Some other small creature or device sent along the rope
A poison let down the rope
